algorithms.title: Search without an index
algorithms.summary: One item in an unsorted list satisfies a hidden yes/no test. Compare checking candidates one at a time with a small Grover experiment you can steer.
algorithms.problem_markdown:
You have N candidate labels. Exactly one of them satisfies a hidden yes/no test f(x). Your job is to return that label.

A **query** is one use of that test. There is no sorted order and no index to exploit: this is the unstructured search problem.

The quantum method needs something stronger than a function you can call. It needs **coherent oracle access**: a reversible quantum operation encoding the same predicate. One quantum query can act on a superposition, but it does not hand you a readable list of every value of the predicate. Building that operation has a cost that sits outside the query count.
algorithms.paradox_note: The experiment generator knows which candidate you selected, because it has to construct the toy oracle. The search procedure is then demonstrated as if it could only reach the oracle. This is an instructional instance, not a useful search for an answer you already have.
algorithms.classical_markdown:
Scanning in increasing order, the queried label, its yes/no answer, and the running query count are shown for each check.

Two stopping rules give different numbers, so we label which one is in use:

- **Check every candidate, including the last:** mean (N+1)/2 checks, worst case N.
- **Use the exactly-one-target promise to infer the final unchecked candidate:** mean (2N-1)/... see the table, worst case N-1.

Both are linear in N.

For a fixed budget of q queries with q < N, a strategy that checks q distinct candidates and guesses one unchecked candidate if all fail succeeds with probability **(q+1)/N**. A strategy that reports only confirmed successes reaches **q/N**. The guessing baseline is included so the comparison does not disadvantage classical search.
algorithms.quantum_markdown:
Standard Grover prepares a uniform superposition, applies a phase oracle, applies a diffusion reflection, repeats that pair k times, then measures one candidate.

**P(target) = sin^2((2k+1) x theta), with theta = arcsin(1/sqrt(N)).**

That expression assumes an ideal noiseless model, exactly one marked state, uniform initial preparation, the specified phase oracle, and the usual diffusion operation. It does not hold for arbitrary initial states.

The useful first probability peak is near k = pi/(4 theta) - 1/2. More iterations can move you past it and make things worse.

The algorithm uses O(sqrt(N)) oracle queries for constant success probability against classical linear query scaling. That is a **quadratic query advantage**. It is not a wall-clock claim about this web demo.
algorithms.worked_example_markdown:
Take N = 4 and mark candidate 2, written |10>. Amplitudes are listed in the order |00>, |01>, |10>, |11>.

| Step | Amplitudes | Probabilities | What to notice |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial register | (1, 0, 0, 0) | (1, 0, 0, 0) | The reset register is a known basis state. |
| Prepare uniformly | (1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2) | (1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4) | Every candidate is equally likely. |
| Oracle | (1/2, 1/2, -1/2, 1/2) | (1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4) | A sign changed. No probability changed. |
| Diffusion | (0, 0, 1, 0) | (0, 0, 1, 0) | The marked outcome now has probability 1. |
| Measurement | recorded outcome 2 | one observed candidate | A shot returns a candidate, not the amplitude table. |

The arithmetic: after the oracle the mean amplitude is 1/4. Diffusion maps each amplitude a to 2 x mean - a. Unmarked amplitudes become 1/2 - 1/2 = 0, and the marked amplitude becomes 1/2 - (-1/2) = 1.
algorithms.overshoot_note: The iteration table is evaluated from the formula above. Those are analytical predictions, not measured counts. Your run's numbers come from the simulator and appear in the result panels.
algorithms.cost_note: One 256-shot Grover histogram at k = 2 represents 256 complete preparations and 512 phase-oracle uses, before any optional candidate verification. It is not a single two-query search. There is no quantum speed multiplier in this app because there is no honest way to compute one here.
algorithms.closing_question: The oracle changed a sign before any probability changed. Why did the next operation make that sign matter?
algorithms.closing_question_note: This is saved as your first Grover mystery. Topic 1.8 returns to it.

preparations.label: What if preparation is missing?
preparations.warning: This variant starts in |0...0> and is explicitly outside the standard success formula. The uniform-start prediction curve does not apply to it, and it is not general amplitude amplification.

algorithms.title: The Shor mystery
algorithms.persistent_label: Conceptual walkthrough with exact classical arithmetic. No Shor circuit is executed.
algorithms.summary: Factoring 15 is easy. We use it to reveal a method that connects factors to a hidden repetition pattern.
algorithms.opening_note: Factoring this tiny number demonstrates nothing about practical speed advantage. It is a way to see the shape of the method.

storyboard.body: Find integers greater than 1 whose product is 15.
Use a = 2. First check gcd(2, 15) = 1, so 2 shares no factor with 15 and is a usable base.
Compute 2^x mod 15 for x = 0 to 7. The results are 1, 2, 4, 8, 1, 2, 4, 8. The pattern repeats.
The smallest positive r with 2^r mod 15 = 1 is r = 4. That r is the order of 2 modulo 15.
Controlled modular operations and phase estimation are the tools that find such an order on a quantum computer. Chapters 9 and 10 build them.
An inverse QFT stage produces a sampled value related to a rational phase. It does not print r directly.
Rational reconstruction and verification turn that sample into an order candidate. Some measurements are unhelpful and the attempt has to be repeated.
With the valid order r = 4, compute gcd(2^2 - 1, 15) = gcd(3, 15) = 3 and gcd(2^2 + 1, 15) = gcd(5, 15) = 5. And 3 x 5 = 15.

algorithms.retry_note: A full lesson has to teach the retries: an unsuitable order, an unhelpful measured phase, or a trivial gcd all send you back for another attempt.
algorithms.complexity_note: Shor's algorithm runs in polynomial time in the input bit length on the theoretical quantum model. A toy demonstration establishes nothing about the physical resources a large instance would need.
algorithms.arithmetic_note: The modular-power table above is explanatory classical arithmetic, computed on the server. Displaying it is not running quantum order finding.

sources.title: Shor, Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms

planned_lab_entries.title: Deutsch
planned_lab_entries.summary: Decide whether a one-bit Boolean function is constant or balanced. One ideal quantum query against two classical queries for exact identification.

planned_lab_entries.title: Bernstein-Vazirani
planned_lab_entries.summary: Recover a hidden n-bit string from a parity oracle. One quantum query against n classical queries for exact recovery.

planned_lab_entries.title: Deutsch-Jozsa
planned_lab_entries.summary: A promise problem with an exponential query separation against exact deterministic classical computation. Bounded-error randomized methods change that comparison.

planned_lab_entries.title: Simon
planned_lab_entries.summary: Measurement supplies constraints orthogonal to a hidden XOR string; a classical linear solve finishes the job.

planned_lab_entries.title: Quantum Fourier transform
planned_lab_entries.summary: A transform on amplitudes. It does not expose an amplitude vector to a single measurement.

planned_lab_entries.title: Quantum phase estimation
planned_lab_entries.summary: Estimates an eigenvalue phase using controlled powers and an inverse QFT. Used inside other algorithms.

planned_lab_entries.title: Teleportation
planned_lab_entries.summary: Transfers a state using an entangled pair and two classical bits. It transports no matter and sends no message faster than light.
